title: Muse Wonder API Pricing for Every Tier and Workload
summary: Muse Wonder API pricing includes plans with different per-token costs. You can choose a tier based on your usage volume and requirements.
body_markdown:
## Muse Wonder API pricing by plan


### Muse Wonder API pricing at a glance


Muse Wonder charges per million tokens, with **separate input and output rates** . Meta lists them at[$1.25 to $4 per million input tokens and $4.25 to $20 per million output tokens](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits) , depending on tier.


As of the 2026-10-15 check, the plan names and the mapping of plans to those rates are unconfirmed, so this article quotes the range and no single figure. A wrong number here would send you into a budget meeting with a figure nobody can defend.


Muse Wonder API pricing is the per-million-token billing model Meta uses to charge for Muse Wonder, with separate input and output rates that vary by plan tier and are subject to that plan's limits and overage rules.


When your software sends text to the model and gets text back through the API, each call bills by tokens: the pieces of text going in (your prompt, the email you paste in) and the pieces coming out (the model's reply).


A call from your own code and a call from a flow in[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) meter the same way at the model, and Activepieces itself costs $0 on its Free plan with unlimited flows on every plan, so the tokens are the part of the bill that varies.


Summarise tickets or write replies to them, and the same plan produces very different bills. That is why input and output have separate prices: a short classification reply costs far less than a long drafted answer.


It is also why the rest of this article prices a workload, not a rate card.


### All plans in one table


Put every plan against the same six questions in a pricing grid:


- monthly price
- input and output price per million tokens
- included usage
- rate limits
- what happens when you go over


Meta's range fills the token-price columns only as a range. We couldn't confirm the plan names, which tier carries which rate, or any other figure, so every plan gets the same answer elsewhere: not stated.


That leaves you the list of what you must still collect yourself before comparing anything.


Build the grid from the vendor's pricing page, one row per plan, with those six columns, before you compare headline rates.


The overage column matters most. A plan that throttles you at the limit and a plan that quietly bills extra are different risks, and the second one is the one that surprises finance.


For this article, the gap is everything:


- plan names
- prices
- included usage
- limits
- overage terms


> A plan that throttles you at the limit and a plan that quietly bills extra are different risks, and the second one is the one that surprises finance.


Treat each as unknown until you see it written on the vendor's page or in your contract.
